hip-replacement.title: Hip Replacement Surgery (Total Hip Arthroplasty)
hip-replacement.lead: Personalised implant selection, surgical planning and recovery guidance. Orthopaedic consultation with Dr Maksym Baida in Kyiv, Ukraine.
hip-replacement.intro: Hip replacement surgery (total hip arthroplasty, THA) may relieve pain and improve mobility when osteoarthritis, osteonecrosis or injury-related damage makes everyday activities difficult and appropriate non-surgical care no longer provides adequate relief. The decision is based on symptoms, function, imaging and individual goals, not an X-ray alone.

body.text: Hip replacement surgery (total hip arthroplasty, THA) may relieve pain and improve mobility when osteoarthritis, osteonecrosis or injury-related damage makes everyday activities difficult and appropriate non-surgical care no longer provides adequate relief. The decision is based on symptoms, function, imaging and individual goals, not an X-ray alone.

Pain can progress from activity-related discomfort to pain during routine walking, at rest or at night. Limping, difficulty with stairs, shoes or getting into a car, and reduced walking distance are common reasons to seek an assessment.
The aim is not simply to insert an implant, but to relieve pain and improve everyday independence and function. Individual outcomes cannot be guaranteed.

blocks.heading: Indications and reasons to defer surgery

items: Symptomatic hip osteoarthritis affecting everyday activities.
Osteonecrosis (avascular necrosis) of the femoral head, particularly with articular collapse.
Post-traumatic arthritis and severe consequences of fractures or dislocations.
Selected proximal femoral fractures where arthroplasty is appropriate.
Severe joint damage due to dysplasia or inflammatory disease.

body.text: Active joint infection or other uncontrolled infection may preclude elective surgery. Uncontrolled cardiac or pulmonary illness, diabetes or other conditions may require assessment and optimisation first. Age or weight alone does not automatically rule out surgery.

For elective surgery, symptoms, functional limitations, structural findings and expected benefit versus non-operative options are considered together. Not everyone with osteoarthritis needs a replacement.
Before surgery, general health, infection risks and opportunities to optimise other conditions should be discussed.

Planning considers hip anatomy, bone quality, acetabular and femoral geometry, leg length and biomechanics. Implant positioning, bearing surfaces and cemented, cementless or hybrid fixation are selected individually. No implant is best for everyone; stability, appropriate component position and functional reconstruction matter.
Preoperative planning includes the hip centre of rotation, leg length, femoral offset and muscle balance. Appropriate component positioning and stability matter alongside implant design.
Fixation and bearing choices are informed by anatomy, bone quality, patient activity and clinical circumstances.

The surgical approach depends on anatomy, pathology and operative goals. A direct anterior approach, sometimes using a skin-crease bikini incision, may be suitable in selected cases. Scar location does not take priority over safety or component positioning, and no approach is universally superior.

Assessment includes symptoms, gait, mobility, leg length and pelvic/hip X-rays; CT or MRI is used when indicated. Health conditions, infection, anaemia, thrombosis and bleeding risks, medications and anaesthetic fitness are reviewed. Do not stop prescribed medicines without medical advice.

During total hip replacement, the damaged femoral head and acetabular surface are replaced with prosthetic components. Anaesthesia is selected individually. Component stability, leg length and range of motion are assessed during surgery. Pain management, complication prevention and early mobilisation follow; walking often starts on the day of surgery or the following day if appropriate.
Optimising blood pressure, blood glucose, anaemia, infection and clotting risks when indicated may reduce complications. Tests and medication adjustments are individual.
After surgery, monitoring, pain relief, venous thromboembolism prevention and tailored weight-bearing guidance are provided.

items: Wound or periprosthetic joint infection, sometimes requiring further surgery.
Deep-vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism.
Dislocation or instability of the new joint.
Periprosthetic fracture during or after surgery.
Leg-length difference, persistent pain or limited movement.
Bleeding or injury to nerves or blood vessels.
Implant wear or loosening, sometimes requiring revision surgery.

body.text: Personal risk varies with medical conditions, anatomy and surgical complexity. Your surgeon will discuss likely benefits, alternatives and risks before surgery.
Persistent pain or residual limitation may also occur. Risks should be discussed according to the individual patient rather than presented as universally applicable guarantees.

items: First days: pain control, wound care, clot prevention and assisted safe walking.
First 2–6 weeks: gradually longer walks, daily activities and muscle strengthening. Weight-bearing advice is individual.
Following months: gradual improvement in strength and endurance; return to work, driving and sport depends on recovery.
Increasing pain, fever, wound discharge or major leg swelling require prompt medical review. Sudden breathlessness, chest pain or fainting require emergency care.

body.text: Rehabilitation supports safe walking, pain control, strength and daily independence. Recovery timelines vary; the phases above are guides, not promises.
Return to driving, employment, sport and travel requires individual advice.

Costs depend on prosthesis components, operative complexity, investigations, anaesthesia, hospital stay, medicines and rehabilitation. An indicative estimate can be discussed after an individual assessment; final costs depend on the agreed treatment plan.
The total estimate may also include anaesthetic care, hospital stay, medicines and postoperative rehabilitation. A fixed amount without a treatment plan would be misleading.

blocks.heading: Clinical case: hip replacement after severe trauma

body.text: The patient is Major Oleksandr Noskovych of the Armed Forces of Ukraine, who sustained a severe hip injury. After initial medical care and five days of staged evacuation, he was admitted to the NMU University Clinic for specialized orthopedic treatment.

Examination revealed a complex injury — a femoral head fracture-dislocation against a background of acetabular dysplasia. Given the nature of the injury, the patient's anatomy, and his functional needs, the decision was made to perform total hip replacement.

The operation was performed using the Direct Anterior Approach (DAA) with a cosmetically oriented bikini incision. The primary goals were to restore hip joint stability, anatomical relationships, and limb function.
X-ray after surgery
Early mobilization began right after surgery: the patient stood up and started walking on the second day, and by the eighth day he was preparing for discharge from the clinic.
This clinical case is featured in an official publication by the O.O. Bohomolets National Medical University Clinic →

blocks.heading: How do I know it's already time for surgery?

body.text: There is no single X-ray finding after which hip replacement automatically becomes necessary.
It's important to assess pain, mobility, walking ability, everyday limitations, and how effective previous treatment has been.

If your hip is making you walk less, give up activities you used to enjoy, rely constantly on painkillers, and treatment no longer provides sufficient relief, it's worth discussing next steps with an orthopedic surgeon.

blocks.heading: Is it still possible to avoid surgery?

body.text: In many cases, yes. The options for conservative or joint-preserving treatment depend on the cause of the condition and the degree of structural change in the joint.
The purpose of a consultation is not to convince the patient that hip replacement is necessary, but to determine whether surgery is genuinely the best treatment option at this point.
There is no universally "best" implant.

Modern systems differ in design, fixation method, and other characteristics. What matters isn't just the implant brand, but choosing the right design for the individual patient, thorough preoperative planning, and precise surgical execution.
Both fixation methods have their indications. The choice depends on age, anatomy, bone quality, and other characteristics specific to the patient.

blocks.heading: Can the operation always be performed through an anterior or bikini approach?

body.text: No. The surgical approach is chosen individually.
The anterior approach and the bikini incision can be used in appropriate clinical situations, but the cosmetic result should never take priority over the safety and quality of the hip replacement.

blocks.heading: Does it hurt a lot after surgery?

body.text: Postoperative pain is expected, especially in the first few days. It is managed with a comprehensive pain control protocol that allows early mobilization to begin.
The intensity of pain and how quickly it subsides vary from patient to patient.

blocks.heading: When will I be able to stand and walk?

body.text: In most cases, mobilization begins in the early postoperative period. Walking aids may be used at first.
The exact weight-bearing regimen depends on the specifics of the operation and the patient's condition.

blocks.heading: Will there be a difference in leg length after surgery?

body.text: Restoring limb length is one of the key goals of preoperative planning and hip replacement itself.
At the same time, in complex clinical cases, anatomical features and the need to ensure joint stability can affect the final outcome.
Recovery happens gradually. In the first few weeks, the main goals are safe walking, gradually increasing activity, and restoring function.
Further improvements in strength, endurance, and confidence in movement can continue over the following months.

blocks.heading: When can I drive a car?

body.text: The timeline depends on which side was operated on, recovery of limb control, the overall course of rehabilitation, and any medications being taken.
The return to driving is determined on an individual basis.

blocks.heading: How long does a hip implant last?

body.text: Modern implants are designed for long-term function. Their lifespan depends on the design and placement of the implant, as well as the patient's age, body weight, physical activity, and other individual factors.

blocks.heading: Can I return to sports and an active life?

body.text: The goal of hip replacement is precisely to help the patient return to a more active life.
Once the main recovery period is complete, many types of physical activity can become available again. Specific loads and sports should be discussed on an individual basis.

knee-replacement.title: Knee Replacement
knee-replacement.lead: Knee replacement for osteoarthritis: total and partial implants, the subvastus approach, planning, risks and recovery in Ukraine.
knee-replacement.intro: Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) replaces damaged joint surfaces with prosthetic components to reduce pain and improve walking and mobility. Decisions depend on symptoms, function, clinical findings and the person's needs, not the radiographic severity alone.

blocks.heading: Knee osteoarthritis and other causes of pain

body.text: Knee osteoarthritis (gonarthrosis) affects cartilage, subchondral bone and other joint structures. Symptoms include pain on walking or stairs, stiffness, swelling, reduced movement and progressive deformity. Pain severity does not always reflect the radiographic findings.

Joint replacement may also be needed for post-traumatic osteoarthritis, advanced inflammatory joint damage including rheumatoid arthritis, osteonecrosis or the consequences of complex deformity. Not every painful knee has osteoarthritis, and not everyone with osteoarthritis needs surgery.

blocks.heading: When should knee replacement be considered?

body.text: Replacement is considered for persistent pain, substantial difficulty with walking and daily life, contracture or progressive deformity associated with advanced structural damage when appropriate non-operative treatment has not helped enough.

Earlier disease is often treated with exercise, activity modification, weight management when appropriate and medication. Once the indication is established, repeated ineffective treatments need not delay surgery without good reason. Decisions are made jointly.

Elective knee replacement should not proceed with active joint infection, bloodstream infection, infection near the surgical field or severe decompensated illness that makes surgery unsafe. Important vascular, neurological or bone conditions require a separate assessment.

Diabetes, anaemia, nutritional problems and modifiable risks including smoking should be addressed. Elevated BMI alone should not automatically rule out assessment. Inform your clinician about recent joint injections, infections, other conditions and medicines.

Total knee arthroplasty (TKA) replaces damaged femoral and tibial articular surfaces using metal components and a polyethylene insert; the patellar surface may also be resurfaced if indicated. The entire knee is not removed. TKA is generally appropriate when several compartments are affected.

Partial or unicompartmental replacement (UKA) resurfaces only one affected compartment, usually medial, preserving other surfaces and some ligament structures. Early recovery may be quicker in properly selected patients, but the method is not suitable for everyone. Arthritis in other compartments may progress and revision may be needed.

Implant selection depends on ligament function, bone quality, deformity and stability. Cruciate-retaining (CR) designs retain a functional posterior cruciate ligament; posterior-stabilised (PS) implants partially substitute its function. More constrained or hinged designs may be necessary in severe instability, bone loss or revision.

Components may be cemented or cementless, with biological fixation. Medical-grade metal alloys and polyethylene are commonly used. No brand, fixation method or design is universally best: positioning, planning and soft-tissue balance are also essential.

We examine pain, gait, flexion, extension, contractures, varus or valgus deformity, ligament stability, the extensor mechanism and previous procedures. Imaging generally includes weight-bearing knee radiographs and, when indicated, standing full-length leg alignment films. CT is used selectively for complex anatomy or particular planning methods.

The mechanical axis connects the centre of the femoral head with the ankle centre. Its position helps assess load distribution. Planning covers component orientation in three planes, joint line height, patellar tracking and ligament balance; decisions may be refined during surgery.

Following preparation and spinal or general anaesthesia, the joint is exposed and planned bone resections are made. Trial implants allow assessment of flexion, extension, stability and patellar tracking. When necessary, soft tissues or insert thickness are adjusted before final implant fixation and wound closure.
A routine primary operation often takes approximately one to two hours; complex cases may take longer. Safety and precision take priority over speed.

blocks.heading: Subvastus surgical approach: preserving the quadriceps

body.text: We preferentially use the subvastus approach, entering beneath vastus medialis without cutting the quadriceps muscle or tendon. In selected patients this may reduce early pain, support quadriceps activation and facilitate mobilisation.

Long-term outcomes of the subvastus and conventional medial parapatellar approaches are broadly comparable. Severe deformity, contracture or difficult anatomy may call for another approach to ensure safe exposure. Muscle preservation must never compromise surgical accuracy.

blocks.heading: Mechanical axis, ligament balance and stability

body.text: The goal is a stable functioning knee, not simply a well-aligned X-ray. Mechanical alignment (MA) follows standard axes; kinematic alignment (KA) considers individual anatomy; restricted KA (rKA) applies defined boundaries; functional alignment (FA) incorporates soft-tissue balance. No approach is proven universally superior over the long term.

During surgery the team assesses medial and lateral tissues, flexion and extension gaps, stability throughout movement and patellar tracking. Exactly identical gaps are not always needed; functional stability without excess tension or laxity matters. Navigation and robotics can support precision but do not guarantee superior long-term outcomes.

Possible complications include periprosthetic infection, deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism, blood loss or anaemia, stiffness, instability, persistent pain, loosening or wear. Periprosthetic fractures and nerve or vessel injuries are less common. Some complications require revision surgery.

Preparation, antibiotics, blood conservation, early mobilisation and individual thrombosis prevention reduce risk. Fever, wound discharge, worsening pain, calf swelling or new sensory or circulation changes require prompt medical review. Sudden breathlessness, chest pain or fainting require emergency assistance.

When safe, standing and walking with support often start on the day of surgery or the following day. The first week focuses on pain and swelling control, extension, gentle flexion and safe walking. During weeks 2–6, strength, balance and stair use improve; during weeks 6–12, activity increases gradually. Recovery may continue for 3–12 months or longer.

Weight-bearing restrictions and walking aids are individual, especially after complex reconstruction. Full or best possible extension and useful flexion matter more than one target angle for everyone. Never force exercises through severe pain. Subvastus access does not eliminate rehabilitation. Driving requires adequate strength, reaction time and safe braking.

Most patients experience less pain and better walking and function after rehabilitation, but a prosthetic knee is not identical to a natural one; stiffness or discomfort may persist. Walking, swimming and cycling are often suitable activities, while running and contact sports need individual discussion.

A large registry-based study (Evans et al., The Lancet, 2019) estimated that about 93%, 90% and 82% of total knee implants had not been revised at 15, 20 and 25 years. These are estimates of freedom from revision, not guaranteed pain-free function. New pain, swelling or instability should be assessed even years later.

The overall cost depends on implant design, surgical complexity, anaesthesia, investigations, inpatient care and rehabilitation. Routine replacement and complex reconstruction for severe deformity or bone defects can have different budgets. A more expensive prosthesis is not necessarily more appropriate.
A preliminary estimate may be provided after a review of available documents; the final quotation follows an examination and an agreed treatment plan. We do not publish an unverified universal price.
Weight-bearing knee and standing full-length leg radiographs

The images show advanced degenerative changes with predominantly medial joint-space narrowing and deformity. Standing full-length radiographs help assess the mechanical axis and plan implant positioning.
Postoperative anteroposterior and lateral knee radiographs

Radiographs from another patient show femoral and tibial prosthetic components. Their positioning can be assessed on X-ray, while function must also be evaluated clinically. Important: these are separate clinical examples, not before-and-after images of the same patient.
When severe pain and functional limitations persist despite appropriate non-surgical treatment; X-ray grading alone is insufficient.
Exercises, activity modification and medication often help earlier disease; advanced symptomatic damage may warrant replacement.

blocks.heading: Can only part of the knee be replaced?

body.text: Yes. UKA may suit isolated single-compartment disease with suitable ligaments and remaining joint structures.
Deformity can be corrected, but the target axis is individualised according to anatomy and stability.

blocks.heading: What makes the subvastus approach different?

body.text: It preserves the quadriceps muscle and tendon and may help early recovery, but it does not suit every patient.

blocks.heading: When can I stand and walk?

body.text: Often on the day of routine surgery or the following day with support, when medically safe.
Active rehabilitation takes weeks; function often improves over 3–6 months and may continue improving for a year.

blocks.heading: Can I bend the knee and climb stairs?

body.text: Movement starts early, with stair practice introduced gradually and safely using a rail and support.
When strength, reaction time and emergency braking are safe and sedating medicines are no longer used.

blocks.heading: Can I kneel and do sports?

body.text: Some patients can kneel after recovery; suitable exercise and high-impact sports need individual advice.

blocks.heading: Can I have an allergy to the implant?

body.text: Clinically important reactions are uncommon; report confirmed material sensitivities. Routine testing is not needed for everyone.
Yes, but simultaneous and staged surgery have different risks and require individual assessment.

blocks.heading: Which implant is best, and how long will it last?

body.text: No single design is universally best. Many implants last 15–20 years or more, without a personal guarantee.

blocks.heading: Can a knee replacement be revised?

body.text: Yes. Infection, loosening, instability, fracture or other problems can require revision.
It depends on the implant, complexity and inpatient care; an individual quotation follows assessment.

blocks.heading: Can I request a consultation from abroad?

body.text: Yes. An initial remote document and imaging review is possible, but final decisions require in-person evaluation.
A consultation considers symptoms, imaging, alignment, stability, alternatives and surgical suitability. Book through the existing contact page.

shoulder-replacement.title: Shoulder Replacement (Anatomic and Reverse Arthroplasty)
shoulder-replacement.lead: Anatomic and reverse shoulder replacement (ATSA/RTSA): indications, planning, surgery, risks and rehabilitation.
shoulder-replacement.intro: Shoulder replacement may be an option when persistent pain and impaired arm function do not improve sufficiently with appropriate non-surgical treatment. Implant selection is individual and depends on the rotator cuff, bone anatomy and functional needs.

body.text: Shoulder replacement is considered for severe glenohumeral osteoarthritis, cuff tear arthropathy, selected complex proximal humerus fractures, post-traumatic arthritis, humeral head osteonecrosis and selected inflammatory conditions. Surgery is not automatically necessary for an isolated cuff tear.

blocks.heading: When should you see an orthopaedic specialist?

body.text: Consult if pain is persistent, particularly at night, arm elevation or self-care is difficult, or movement and strength deteriorate despite treatment. Clinical symptoms and imaging inform the decision.

ATSA restores near-natural joint geometry; RTSA reverses the ball-and-socket configuration to enable the deltoid to contribute more effectively to arm elevation. Rotator cuff function, glenoid bone stock and patient needs guide the selection.

ATSA replaces the humeral head and glenoid articular surface while retaining anatomical relationships. It generally requires an adequately functioning rotator cuff and stable bone support. Massive irreparable cuff damage may limit its suitability.

RTSA attaches the spherical component to the glenoid and the concave socket to the humerus. Indications include cuff tear arthropathy, painful irreparable cuff tears, selected pseudoparalysis, complex fractures, major glenoid deformity and some revisions. Full motion, especially external rotation, cannot be promised.

blocks.heading: The importance of the rotator cuff

body.text: The supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis stabilise the shoulder. Evaluation covers tendon integrity, retraction, atrophy, fatty degeneration and deltoid function. Age alone does not determine ATSA versus RTSA.

Examination assesses pain, active and passive movement, cuff strength, deltoid and nerve function. Radiographs assess arthritis, deformity and prior injuries. CT provides detail on glenoid version, inclination, erosion and bone defects. MRI or ultrasound may be used for tendons and muscles.

In complex anatomy, CT-based three-dimensional planning helps evaluate glenoid shape, implant size and orientation, fixation, potential bone grafts, augments or patient-specific guides. This does not guarantee improved clinical results.

Implant selection considers cuff function, bone quality, humeral and glenoid anatomy, defects and prior operations. Stemmed, stemless and augmented components may be appropriate in different cases; stable fixation is more important than brand.

Surgery is performed with appropriate anaesthesia, commonly through a deltopectoral approach. Components are prepared, positioned and tested for stability. Subscapularis repair may matter in ATSA; glenosphere placement, baseplate fixation and soft-tissue balance matter in RTSA.

Potential complications include infection (including indolent Cutibacterium acnes infection), instability or dislocation, component loosening, periprosthetic fracture, nerve injury, haematoma, wound problems, thromboembolism and stiffness.

blocks.heading: Complications specific to ATSA and RTSA

body.text: ATSA-specific concerns include subscapularis or other rotator cuff failure and glenoid wear or loosening. RTSA-specific issues include instability, acromial or scapular spine stress fractures and scapular notching, which does not always cause symptoms.

Risk reduction involves correct indications, management of comorbidities and active infections, surgical planning, component fixation, infection prevention, individual rehabilitation and follow-up. Risks cannot be completely removed.

Pain relief and improved function are primary goals. ATSA can preserve near-natural mechanics with a competent cuff; RTSA may improve elevation with cuff deficiency but external rotation may stay restricted. Implants can last many years without a guaranteed lifespan.

Seek urgent advice for fever and wound drainage, sudden severe pain or deformity, abrupt functional decline or new marked numbness. Chest pain or significant shortness of breath requires emergency care.
Recovery protects healing tissues and gradually restores arm control. A sling may be used initially, with hand and wrist movement early and shoulder exercise only as allowed by the surgical protocol.

Approximately 0–6 weeks: tissue protection and allowed assisted movement. At 6–12 weeks: progressive active movement. At 3–6 months: gradual muscle strengthening. Functional improvements may continue for 6–12 months or longer; timelines are individual.
Following ATSA, a repaired subscapularis may require restrictions on external rotation, resisted internal rotation, pushing, lifting and stretching during early healing.

Following RTSA, rehabilitation focuses on deltoid and scapular control. Early combined extension, adduction and internal rotation or pushing up from a chair may risk instability. Fracture and revision cases often require modified protocols.

Return to self-care, driving, work and sport is gradual. Driving requires adequate control, no sling and clinician approval. Heavy lifting, contact sports and high-impact activity may remain unsuitable.

Review pain, wound, motion, strength, component position and radiographs at follow-up. Patients returning abroad should arrange local rehabilitation and visits before surgery; remote advice cannot replace in-person care.

blocks.heading: Reverse shoulder replacement following severe trauma

body.text: An Ukrainian serviceman experienced severe post-traumatic shoulder arthritis with persistent pain and functional loss. Reverse shoulder replacement was performed at Bogomolets National Medical University University Clinic by orthopaedic trauma surgeon Maksym Baida. Its purpose was pain relief and improved potential function; no unverified individual long-term result is claimed.
Preoperative and postoperative radiographs
Official NMU clinical case publication
When marked joint damage causes persistent pain and impaired function despite appropriate treatment; assessment is individual.

blocks.heading: Can arthritis be managed without surgery?

body.text: Medication, exercise and activity adjustment can help symptoms in some patients, but cannot restore severely damaged articular surfaces.

blocks.heading: Anatomic or reverse shoulder replacement: which is better?

body.text: Neither is universally superior. Rotator cuff function, glenoid anatomy and the underlying condition determine the choice.
X-rays are essential; CT assesses glenoid anatomy and MRI or ultrasound may evaluate tendons when indicated.

blocks.heading: Will I regain full arm movement?

body.text: Improvement is possible but normal shoulder motion cannot be guaranteed, particularly external rotation after RTSA.
Pain is expected initially and treated with an individual pain-control plan; unexpected worsening warrants review.

blocks.heading: How long must I wear a sling?

body.text: Often several weeks, depending on the operation and repaired tissues. Follow your surgeon's protocol.
Hand and permitted elbow movements start early; shoulder movement follows individual instructions.
Recovery continues over months, sometimes 6–12 months or longer.
Some activities can resume after rehabilitation; heavy or contact sports may be discouraged.

blocks.heading: How long does a shoulder implant last?

body.text: It can function many years, but no individual lifespan is guaranteed. Regular reviews matter.
An initial remote review of medical documents may be possible, but definitive decisions need an appropriate clinical examination.

Dr Maksym Baida assesses shoulder symptoms, imaging, rotator cuff and treatment options. Not every painful shoulder requires replacement. Patients from Kyiv, other regions and abroad may request a consultation.

arthroscopy.title: Arthroscopic Surgery
arthroscopy.lead: Minimally invasive surgical treatment of knee and shoulder joint injuries through small incisions — with precise intra-articular diagnosis and repair of damaged structures.
arthroscopy.intro: Pain, swelling, instability, locking, or restricted movement in a joint don't always require major open surgery.

body.text: In many cases, injuries to the menisci, ligaments, tendons, and other joint structures can be treated with arthroscopic surgery.
But arthroscopy is not needed for every joint pain. The decision to operate is made after establishing the cause of the symptoms and assessing whether surgery can genuinely improve function.
Arthroscopy is a minimally invasive surgical technique in which a special optical instrument — an arthroscope — is inserted into the joint through a small incision.
The image of the joint's internal structures is displayed on a monitor, allowing the surgeon to assess them in detail.
Through additional small incisions, specialized instruments are inserted to perform the necessary surgical procedure.

In this way, arthroscopy not only allows the pathology inside the joint to be visualized, but in appropriate cases also allows damaged structures to be repaired or reconstructed through minimal surgical access.
A consultation with an orthopedic surgeon is worthwhile if you are experiencing:

items: pain in the knee or shoulder joint
recurring joint swelling after exertion
a sensation of locking or the knee "catching"
instability or a feeling that the knee is "giving way"
shoulder pain when raising the arm
shoulder weakness after an injury
repeated dislocations or instability of the shoulder joint
restricted range of motion
the after-effects of a sports injury
symptoms that persist despite conservative treatment

body.text: The first step is to establish the cause of the symptoms.
Only after that can it be determined whether arthroscopic surgery is needed.
The knee is one of the joints where arthroscopic techniques are especially widely used.
The menisci play an important role in load distribution and stability of the knee joint.
A meniscus tear can occur after an injury, presenting with pain, swelling, clicking, or mechanical locking of the knee.
Not every tear requires surgery.
When arthroscopic treatment is indicated, the key question is:

items: can the meniscus be preserved?

body.text: In appropriate cases, preference is given to repair and meniscal suture. If the nature of the injury does not allow this, only the unstable, damaged portion may be removed.
The goal is to preserve as much functional meniscal tissue as possible, rather than simply removing it.
A tear of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) can cause knee instability, especially during running, sudden changes of direction, and sporting activity.
The decision to reconstruct depends on more than just the MRI.
The following are taken into account:

items: clinical instability
age
level of physical activity
sporting and occupational demands
concomitant meniscal and cartilage injuries
patient expectations

body.text: If surgery is indicated, ligament reconstruction is performed to restore stability of the knee joint.
Arthroscopy can also be used for certain localized injuries to the joint cartilage, loose intra-articular bodies, and other pathological conditions.
The approach is determined by the nature of the defect, the patient's age, and the overall condition of the joint.
Shoulder pain can be related to various structures — the rotator cuff tendons, the labrum, ligaments, and other components of the shoulder complex.
That is why it is important to identify the specific source of the problem before surgery.
The rotator cuff is a group of tendons that provide stability and movement of the shoulder joint.
Damage to it can cause:

items: pain
night pain
weakness
difficulty raising the arm
reduced shoulder function

body.text: Not every tear requires surgery.
But when indicated, the damaged tendon can be repaired arthroscopically and fixed back to the bone.
After a traumatic shoulder dislocation, the structures that provide joint stability may be damaged.
In some patients, repeated episodes of instability occur after the first dislocation.
This is especially relevant for young and physically active people.
In appropriate cases, arthroscopic surgery allows the damaged stabilizing structures to be repaired.
It is important to assess not only the soft tissues but also any potential bone loss, since a significant bone defect may require a different reconstructive strategy.
This is one of the key questions addressed on this page.
Not every meniscus tear needs surgery.
Not every rotator cuff tear requires immediate surgery.
Not every joint pain can be cured with arthroscopy.
The decision depends on the cause of the symptoms, the nature of the injury, age, activity level, duration of the problem, and the results of prior treatment.
The mere presence of changes on an MRI does not automatically mean surgery is necessary.
We treat the patient and the impairment of their joint function — not the MRI image.

blocks.heading: MRI showed a tear — what's next?

body.text: MRI reports often contain wording that sounds alarming to a patient: "meniscus tear," "degenerative changes," "cartilage damage," "tendon tear."
But an MRI result needs to be assessed together with:

items: your symptoms
the history of the injury
clinical examination
age
physical activity
the overall condition of the joint

body.text: Sometimes the changes described on an MRI are not the main cause of the pain.
So an MRI helps inform the decision, but it does not make that decision instead of the doctor.
The outcome depends on the specific condition and the type of procedure.
The goal of arthroscopic treatment may be:

items: reducing pain
eliminating mechanical locking
restoring stability
repairing a damaged meniscus
reconstructing a ligament
repairing a tendon
improving range of motion
returning to everyday and sporting activity

body.text: It is important to understand that arthroscopy cannot "make the joint new" and does not eliminate every cause of pain.
This is especially true for advanced arthritis, where the problem is no longer a single damaged structure but significant, widespread damage to the joint as a whole.
We identify the nature of the symptoms, the mechanism of injury, activity level, and functional limitations.
We perform clinical tests to assess specific joint structures.
Depending on the condition, X-ray, MRI, and in certain cases CT scans are used.
We determine whether the problem can be treated conservatively, or whether surgery offers a clear, justified advantage.
The necessary procedure is performed through small incisions, according to the pathology identified.
Rehabilitation depends on the surgery performed.
After a minor procedure, recovery can be relatively quick. After a meniscal repair, ligament reconstruction, or rotator cuff repair, a longer, supervised process is required.
The decision to operate is made based on a combination of symptoms, clinical examination, and imaging results.
A change seen on MRI is not, by itself, an indication for arthroscopy.

blocks.heading: We preserve what can be preserved

body.text: If a meniscus or other structure can reasonably be repaired, a tissue-sparing approach is preferred.

blocks.heading: We restore function, not just fix damage

body.text: The end goal is a stable, mobile, and functional joint.

blocks.heading: We plan rehabilitation together with the surgery

body.text: The outcome of ligament reconstruction, meniscal repair, or tendon repair depends heavily on properly structured post-operative recovery.

blocks.heading: We don't offer arthroscopy where it won't solve the problem

body.text: In cases of advanced arthritis or other significant structural damage to the joint, arthroscopic surgery may not deliver the expected result.
In such situations, it is important to identify a different, more suitable treatment option.

blocks.heading: A complex recurrent knee injury after previous surgery

body.text: The patient had previously undergone surgical treatment of the knee. During a follow-up MRI, a complete rupture of the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) graft was found, together with a vertical tear of the lateral meniscus and a meniscocapsular injury of the posterior horn of the medial meniscus (a ramp lesion).
The MRI also showed associated post-traumatic and post-surgical changes.

MRI of both knees. Right — a repeat injury to the anterior cruciate ligament graft along with associated meniscal injuries after previous surgical treatment; left — a comparative scan of the other knee.

blocks.heading: What matters in a situation like this?

body.text: Even findings this pronounced on MRI do not, by themselves, determine the final treatment strategy. The imaging results must be weighed together with the patient's complaints, the clinical stability of the knee, level of physical activity, the outcome of the previous surgery, and functional needs.
Only after this comprehensive assessment can it be determined whether repeat surgery is needed, which structures require repair, and what scope of surgery would be appropriate.
MRI shows the structure of the injury. The surgeon's task is to determine its clinical significance and choose the right treatment strategy.

blocks.heading: Have you been recommended arthroscopic surgery?

body.text: If the surgery is elective and the clinical situation allows time for a decision, you can get a second opinion on the proposed treatment.
This can be especially useful if:

items: surgery was recommended based on the MRI alone
it is unclear whether conservative treatment could be tried first
removal of part of the meniscus has been proposed
there is uncertainty about whether ligament reconstruction is needed
rotator cuff surgery has been recommended
the symptoms and MRI findings do not seem fully clear to you

body.text: During the consultation, the MRI results can be weighed against your symptoms and clinical picture to determine whether surgery is really needed and what problem it should solve.

blocks.heading: Can arthroscopy be done just for diagnosis?

body.text: Modern MRI and other imaging methods provide a great deal of information without surgery.
That's why arthroscopy is usually planned when there is a specific surgical task to accomplish, not simply to "look inside the joint."

blocks.heading: If the MRI shows a meniscus tear, does it always need surgery?

body.text: No.
The approach depends on the type of tear, symptoms, age, mechanism of injury, and the overall condition of the knee joint.

blocks.heading: Is it better to remove or repair the meniscus?

body.text: If the nature of the injury, its location, and tissue quality allow for acceptable healing conditions, preserving the meniscus may be the priority.
But not every tear is technically and biologically suitable for repair.

blocks.heading: How long does arthroscopic surgery take?

body.text: The duration depends on the procedure.
A simple arthroscopic procedure and a complex ACL or rotator cuff reconstruction are fundamentally different operations.

blocks.heading: When can I walk after knee arthroscopy?

body.text: This depends on exactly what was done.
After some procedures, weight-bearing is allowed early on; after others, it must be temporarily restricted to protect the repaired structure.

blocks.heading: When can I drive a car?

body.text: The timeline depends on which joint was operated on, the side of the surgery, the nature of the procedure, control of the limb, and use of pain medication.
Returning to driving should be based on safety, not just the number of days since surgery.

blocks.heading: When can I return to sport?

body.text: This depends on the surgery.

After ligament reconstruction or tendon repair, return to sport is a separate stage of rehabilitation, determined not just by time since surgery but by the recovery of strength, stability, and functional performance.
Yes, but arthroscopic incisions are usually small.
The number and location of scars depend on the specific surgery.
In advanced arthritis, arthroscopic surgery usually cannot address the underlying problem — significant wear of the joint surfaces.
That's why it is important, before surgery, to determine whether there is a specific pathology that arthroscopic treatment can genuinely correct.

blocks.heading: Do I need an MRI before the consultation?

body.text: Not always.
If an MRI has already been done, it's best to bring not just the report but the images themselves.
If the scan hasn't been done yet, in some cases it is better to have an examination first and then obtain the necessary imaging afterward.

blocks.heading: Is your knee or shoulder hurting?

body.text: If pain, instability, locking, or restricted movement don't go away, the first step is to identify the structure causing the problem and understand whether it requires surgical treatment.
If an MRI has already been done, or arthroscopy has already been recommended to you, the consultation can be used to review the results, discuss alternatives, and determine a possible strategy.
Arthroscopy is a tool. What matters most is correctly identifying the problem that tool is meant to solve.

hallux-valgus.title: Hallux Valgus (Bunion)
hallux-valgus.lead: Modern surgical correction of first-toe deformity — to reduce pain and restore function and the foot's natural shape.
hallux-valgus.intro: If the bunion is getting bigger, shoes are becoming uncomfortable, or pain or deformity of the other toes has appeared, it's worth assessing the degree of change and determining the best treatment strategy.

blocks.heading: When a bunion is no longer just a cosmetic problem

body.text: Hallux valgus (bunion) is a deformity of the forefoot in which the big toe gradually deviates toward the other toes, and a characteristic bony prominence forms at the first metatarsophalangeal joint.
This is not simply a local bony enlargement. The relative position of the bones, the biomechanics of the forefoot, and the distribution of load during walking all change.

In its early stages, the problem may mainly affect appearance. As the deformity progresses, pain, redness, and irritation around the bunion may appear, along with difficulty finding comfortable shoes, calluses, and deformity of the other toes.

items: the bunion is gradually getting bigger
the big toe is increasingly deviating
pain has appeared while walking or standing for long periods
shoes press and rub against the deformity
it's becoming difficult to find comfortable shoes
calluses or areas of overload on the foot are appearing
the second and other toes are starting to deform
the shape of the foot is causing significant functional or cosmetic discomfort

body.text: The goal of modern surgical correction of hallux valgus is not simply to remove the bony prominence.
Surgery aims to correct the deformity itself and restore more normal anatomical alignment of the forefoot.
After surgery and an appropriate recovery period, treatment can help:

items: reduce pain at the base of the big toe
correct its abnormal deviation
reduce the prominence of the bunion
improve the shape of the foot
improve load distribution across the forefoot
reduce discomfort when wearing shoes
gradually return to normal walking and physical activity

body.text: The goal of treatment is to combine functional correction of the deformity with the most natural possible foot shape.
Modern surgery is not simply "shaving off the bunion"
One common misconception is to think of hallux valgus surgery as simply removing the bony prominence.
The cause of the deformity is far more complex. The position of the forefoot bones themselves changes, so simply removing the prominent part of the bone is not enough for a complete correction.
Modern surgical treatment is aimed at correcting the underlying anatomical deformity, not just its outward appearance.
That's why it is important, before surgery, to determine the nature and degree of the deformity and to plan the method of correction.
Hallux valgus can look similar from the outside in different patients, yet have different underlying anatomical features.
Before surgery, we assess:

items: the degree of deviation of the big toe
the relative position of the forefoot bones
the condition of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
the stability of the relevant joints
the position of the other toes
any accompanying foot deformities
load distribution and clinical symptoms

body.text: Weight-bearing X-rays of the foot are taken for planning purposes.
The optimal method of correction is determined based on the clinical examination and radiographic parameters.
There is no single hallux valgus operation that suits every patient equally.
Depending on the nature and degree of the deformity, various types of corrective osteotomies and other surgical techniques may be used.
The procedure may involve repositioning the first metatarsal bone and the big toe, restoring normal anatomical alignment, and stabilizing the bone fragments with special fixation devices.
If other forefoot deformities are present at the same time, these can also be taken into account when planning the surgery.
The surgical method is chosen to fit the specific deformity — not the other way around.

blocks.heading: Function and the appearance of the foot

body.text: For many patients, what matters is not only reducing pain, but also how the foot will look after surgery.
This is a normal part of what patients expect from treatment.
When planning, we aim to combine two goals:
restoring more normal anatomical alignment and function of the foot, and achieving the most natural possible shape.
A good cosmetic result is founded on correct anatomical correction of the deformity.
We assess your complaints, the shape of the foot, the position of the big toe and other toes, painful areas, and features of your gait.
We analyze weight-bearing X-rays of the foot and determine the nature of the deformity.
Based on the anatomy and radiographic parameters, we determine which components of the deformity need to be corrected and which surgical technique best fits the specific case.
The deformity is corrected, restoring normal anatomical alignment of the forefoot and stabilizing it according to the chosen technique.
After surgery, a weight-bearing regimen and the use of a post-operative shoe are determined, along with a gradual return to normal walking and everyday activity.
We correct the deformity, not just the bunion
Our surgical strategy is aimed at correcting the anatomical components of hallux valgus, not simply removing the visible bony prominence.
Bone position is assessed under the conditions in which the foot actually functions during standing and walking.
The degree and type of deformity can vary, so the same operation should not be applied to every patient.
When planning the correction, we consider not only the functional outcome but also the natural appearance of the foot.

blocks.heading: Can a bunion be treated without surgery?

body.text: Conservative methods can help reduce symptoms and discomfort, especially in the early stages.
Changing your footwear, orthotic devices, and other measures can ease pain, but they generally cannot anatomically correct a bony deformity that has already formed.
If the deformity is progressing and is significantly bothering you, the possibility of surgical correction is worth discussing with an orthopedic surgeon.

blocks.heading: Do I need to wait until the bunion gets very large?

body.text: No. The size of the bunion alone is not the only indication for surgery.
The decision depends on pain, progression of the deformity, difficulties with footwear, the condition of the other toes, and the patient's expectations.

blocks.heading: Can I have surgery if I'm mainly bothered by how my foot looks?

body.text: Cosmetic discomfort can be one of the reasons for seeking treatment.
However, before deciding on surgery, it is important to assess the deformity itself, the expected benefit, the possible risks, and how realistic the expected result is.

blocks.heading: Is the surgery just shaving off the bunion?

body.text: No. In most cases, complete correction of hallux valgus involves repositioning the bone structures and restoring normal anatomical alignment.
That's why the surgery is planned based on clinical and radiographic findings.

blocks.heading: Are screws placed during the surgery?

body.text: Special fixation devices, including screws, may be used to stabilize the correction.
Whether fixation is needed, and what type, depends on the surgical technique chosen.

blocks.heading: When can I put weight on my foot?

body.text: The weight-bearing regimen depends on the correction performed and the method of fixation.
In many cases, walking is possible early in the post-operative period using a special post-operative shoe, but the specific regimen is determined individually.

blocks.heading: How long do I need to wear the special shoe?

body.text: The duration depends on the type of surgery and how healing progresses. The transition back to regular shoes happens gradually, after appropriate follow-up.

blocks.heading: When will my foot look normal after surgery?

body.text: Swelling can persist for quite a long time after surgery, so the final shape of the foot should not be judged in the first few weeks.
As healing progresses and swelling subsides, the appearance gradually changes.
Any surgical procedure leaves a scar.
Its location and length depend on the surgical technique used. Over time, a post-operative scar usually fades and becomes less noticeable, but its final appearance cannot be fully predicted.
Recurrence of the deformity is possible.
The risk depends on many factors, including the original type of deformity, how correctly it was corrected, individual anatomical features, and how the post-operative period progresses.
That's why it is important not simply to remove the visible bunion, but to correctly identify and correct the components of the deformity.

blocks.heading: When can I go back to regular shoes?

body.text: This depends on the extent of the surgery, healing, and swelling. The return to regular footwear happens gradually.
In the early period, it's best to choose roomy, comfortable shoes that don't put pressure on the forefoot.

blocks.heading: Can I wear high heels after surgery?

body.text: Returning to this type of footwear depends on how recovery has progressed, the condition of the foot, and the height of the heel.
It's best to discuss the possibility and timing individually once the main recovery period is complete.

If a bunion is painful, growing, making it hard to wear your usual shoes, or if the shape of your foot is bothering you, a consultation lets us assess the nature of the deformity and the possible ways to correct it.
Not every patient with hallux valgus needs surgery. Our task is to determine whether surgical treatment is needed and which method of correction would be optimal for your specific situation.

avn.title: Avascular Necrosis of the Femoral Head
avn.lead: A condition in which timely diagnosis can fundamentally influence treatment choice and the possibility of preserving your own hip joint.
avn.intro: If you have developed pain in the groin or hip joint, and an MRI has revealed avascular necrosis, it's important not only to confirm the diagnosis but also to determine the stage of the disease and the condition of the femoral head. This largely determines the further treatment strategy.

body.text: Avascular necrosis (also known as aseptic necrosis) of the femoral head is a condition in which the blood supply to an area of bone tissue in the femoral head is disrupted.

In the early stages, the shape of the femoral head may still be preserved. As the disease progresses, the bone loses strength, which can lead to a subchondral fracture and gradual flattening or collapse of the femoral head.
After this, the geometry of the hip joint changes and secondary osteoarthritis develops.
This is why avascular necrosis should be viewed not simply as a diagnosis, but as a process with different stages and different treatment options.

blocks.heading: When You Should See a Doctor

items: pain has appeared in the groin or hip joint without an obvious injury
pain occurs during walking or exertion
hip joint mobility has decreased
you have developed a limp
the pain is gradually increasing
an MRI or X-ray has revealed signs of avascular necrosis
avascular necrosis has already been diagnosed, but you need to determine further treatment strategy
both hip joints are affected

blocks.heading: Why It's Important to Determine the Stage of the Disease

body.text: With avascular necrosis, the same diagnosis label can describe fundamentally different clinical situations.
In the early stage, the femoral head may still retain its shape. In such situations, certain patients may be candidates for methods aimed at preserving their own hip joint.

If collapse of the femoral head has already occurred and pronounced secondary joint changes have formed, the possibilities for joint-preserving treatment become significantly limited, and hip replacement may need to be considered.
So the key question after diagnosis is not simply "is there necrosis?" but "what stage is it at, and can the joint still be preserved?"
No.
The mere presence of avascular necrosis does not automatically mean the patient needs hip replacement.
Treatment strategy depends on:

items: the stage of the disease
the size and location of the affected area
whether the shape of the femoral head is preserved
the condition of the joint cartilage
the patient's age
level of physical activity
severity of pain and functional limitations

body.text: This is why treatment decisions should be made after a comprehensive evaluation, not simply based on the words "avascular necrosis" appearing in an MRI report.
If the disease is detected before significant collapse of the femoral head, methods aimed at preserving the patient's own joint may be considered in appropriate clinical situations.
The specific strategy depends on the stage and characteristics of the necrotic area.

One surgical approach used in the early stages is core decompression of the femoral head. Its goal is to create channels in the affected area and attempt to influence the course of the disease process before significant deformity of the femoral head develops.
In certain situations, other joint-preserving techniques may also be considered.
Their potential depends most heavily on how early the diagnosis was made and whether the structure of the femoral head is preserved.

If the disease has progressed, collapse of the femoral head has occurred, and significant structural changes have formed in the hip joint, joint-preserving methods may no longer provide the expected result.
In such cases, one treatment option is total hip replacement.
The goal of the operation is to reduce pain, restore mobility, and return the patient to a more active daily life.
Thus, with the same diagnosis, two patients may be recommended completely different strategies:

items: early stage → attempt to preserve the patient's own joint
late stage → hip replacement

body.text: We assess the nature and duration of the pain, hip joint mobility, gait, prior treatment, and possible factors related to the development of the disease.
We analyze X-rays and MRI scans of the hip joints.
MRI is especially important in the early stages, when structural changes may not yet be clearly visible on a standard X-ray.
We assess the condition of the femoral head, the presence or absence of collapse, the extent of the affected area, and secondary joint changes.
We determine whether there are grounds for joint-preserving treatment, or whether the changes are already so pronounced that hip replacement is the more appropriate option.
We don't just treat an "MRI report"
It's important to correlate imaging findings with the patient's complaints, joint function, and the stage of the disease process.

blocks.heading: We First Assess Whether the Joint Can Be Preserved

body.text: Especially in young and active patients, it's important to determine whether real options remain for joint-preserving treatment.

A method that may be appropriate at an early stage may no longer make sense after collapse of the femoral head. Conversely, hip replacement should not automatically become the first choice simply because a diagnosis has been made.

blocks.heading: From Diagnosis to a Concrete Plan

body.text: The goal of the consultation is not simply to confirm the presence of avascular necrosis, but to answer the patient's main question: what to do next in their specific situation.

blocks.heading: Is Avascular Necrosis the Same as Hip Osteoarthritis?

body.text: No. These are different pathological processes.

In avascular necrosis, the bone tissue of the femoral head is primarily affected. As the disease progresses and the head becomes deformed, secondary osteoarthritic changes in the hip joint may develop.

blocks.heading: Can Avascular Necrosis Resolve on Its Own?

body.text: This disease requires monitoring and assessment of the risk of progression. The strategy depends on the stage, the size of the affected area, and clinical symptoms.
You should not rely on the hope that diagnosed avascular necrosis will resolve on its own.

blocks.heading: If My X-ray Is Normal, Can I Still Have Necrosis?

body.text: Yes. In the early stages, changes may not be clearly visible on standard X-rays.
In the relevant clinical situation, MRI can be especially important for early diagnosis.

blocks.heading: If Necrosis Was Found on MRI, Do I Already Need Surgery?

body.text: Not necessarily.

First, it's necessary to determine the stage, size, and location of the affected area, the condition of the femoral head, and the clinical symptoms. Only after that can the optimal strategy be discussed.

blocks.heading: Can My Own Hip Joint Be Preserved?

body.text: In some patients at early stages, this possibility may be considered.
The chances and appropriateness of joint-preserving treatment depend primarily on the stage of the disease and whether the structure of the femoral head is preserved.
This is a joint-preserving surgical procedure in which one or several channels are created in the head and neck of the femur.
The method may be considered for certain patients in the early stages of the disease. Its appropriateness is determined individually.

blocks.heading: Why Is It Important Not to Delay a Consultation?

body.text: Because the possibilities for joint-preserving treatment depend on the stage of the disease.
After significant collapse of the femoral head develops, the choice of methods aimed at preserving the patient's own joint narrows considerably.

blocks.heading: Are Both Hip Joints Often Affected?

body.text: Bilateral involvement is possible. That's why, once the diagnosis is established, it's important to assess the overall clinical picture and, if indicated, examine the other hip joint.

blocks.heading: If the Femoral Head Is Already Destroyed, What Can Be Done?

body.text: In cases of significant collapse and secondary joint changes, the appropriateness of total hip replacement is assessed.
The decision depends on symptoms, the degree of structural changes, age, activity level, and other individual factors.
If your MRI or X-ray report already indicates avascular necrosis of the femoral head, it's important to determine the stage of the disease and the possibilities for preserving your own joint.
During the consultation, we will assess the results of your examinations, the condition of the hip joint, and determine the possible options for further treatment.
Avascular necrosis does not automatically mean you need hip replacement. Our task is to determine which treatment will be optimal for your specific stage of the disease.

trauma-reconstruction.title: Reconstruction of Post-Traumatic Conditions
trauma-reconstruction.lead: Reconstructive surgical treatment after complex fractures and injuries — when a bone has healed incorrectly, a fracture fails to unite, a limb is deformed or shortened, or its function remains limited.
trauma-reconstruction.intro: An injury and the initial surgery do not always mark the end of treatment. If pain, deformity, limping, limb shortening, or difficulty walking and bearing weight persist after a fracture, reconstructive treatment is possible in many cases.

blocks.heading: The injury is behind you, but function hasn't returned

body.text: After complex fractures, the main goal of the first stage of treatment is often to stabilize the injured limb and create the conditions for healing.
However, the further course of recovery can vary.

A fracture may fail to unite, or it may heal in an incorrect position. Deformity, shortening, a shift in limb axis, restricted movement, or pain may remain. After multi-stage treatment, bone defects or problems related to previously placed hardware can also occur.
In such situations, the question is no longer simply "has the fracture healed?" but how fully the anatomy and function of the limb have been restored.

items: the fracture has not healed for an extended period
the bone has healed with a deformity
the limb has become shorter after the injury
the axis of the leg or arm has changed
limping persists
there is pain when walking or bearing weight
movement in the adjacent joints remains restricted
hardware that was placed is causing problems or has lost stability
limb function remains unsatisfactory after several previous operations
a post-traumatic bone defect has formed
you need a repeat assessment of reconstructive treatment options

body.text: The goal of reconstruction is not simply to perform another operation.
First, it's necessary to determine exactly which consequences of the injury are currently limiting the limb's function, and only then build a plan to correct them.
Depending on the specific situation, reconstructive treatment may be aimed at:

items: achieving union of a nonunion fracture
correcting a malunion
restoring limb axis
eliminating or reducing pathological rotation
correcting shortening
restoring stability
reconstructing a bone defect
improving the limb's ability to bear weight
improving gait and everyday function

body.text: The main goal is not simply to improve the appearance of an X-ray, but to restore the limb's function as fully as possible.
If bone fragments have healed in an incorrect position, a post-traumatic deformity can develop.

Externally, this is sometimes visible as curvature or shortening of the limb. In other cases the deformity is less obvious, but it still changes biomechanics, load distribution, and the function of neighboring joints.
In such situations, surgical correction of the bone's position followed by stabilization in the planned position may be considered.
It's important to evaluate not only the site of the original fracture, but the whole limb as a single biomechanical system.
If a fracture is not showing proper healing within the expected time frame, the cause needs to be identified.

Both mechanical and biological conditions are important for successful union. So the problem may be related to the stability of fixation, the nature of a bone defect, tissue condition, blood supply, or other factors.
A repeat operation in this situation should not simply replace one piece of hardware with another — it should address the causes preventing union.
After complex fractures, a difference in limb length, an angular deformity, or a rotational deformity can remain.
This can show up as limping, fatigue, an altered gait, pain, and overload of neighboring joints.
Before reconstruction, it's important to accurately determine:

items: the degree of shortening
the location and severity of the deformity
the condition of the joints
the quality of the bone tissue
the condition of the soft tissues
previous operations and any hardware that was placed

body.text: After this, it's possible to determine whether deformity correction, length restoration, or a combination of both is needed.
With high-energy injuries, after multi-stage treatment, or after repeated operations, a significant bone defect can develop.
Such cases require separate reconstructive planning.
Depending on the nature of the defect, multi-stage reconstruction methods, bone grafting, defect-replacement techniques, and individualized reconstructive solutions may be used.
Critical bone defects are a dedicated focus of our work, so a specialized page describing treatment options for them in more detail is available.

blocks.heading: Why a repeat operation needs new planning

body.text: After one or more previous operations, the anatomy may already differ significantly from what it was immediately after the injury.
There may be:

items: previously placed hardware
bone defects
scarring
axis or length abnormalities
contractures
changes in soft-tissue condition
the consequences of previous surgical interventions

body.text: So a reconstructive operation shouldn't be seen simply as "redoing the previous one."
It's a new clinical situation that requires a new treatment plan.
We review the history of the injury, previous operations, X-rays, and other examinations.
It's important to understand not only the limb's current state, but also how it developed.
We determine exactly what is limiting function: nonunion, deformity, shortening, instability, a bone defect, joint condition, or a combination of several problems.
We build the treatment sequence: what needs to be corrected, whether it can be done in one operation or requires multi-stage treatment, and which method of stabilization is optimal.
The planned correction is carried out, restoring anatomy, stability, length, or bone continuity according to the specific clinical situation.
After surgery, a loading regimen and a functional recovery program are defined. Their duration depends on the complexity of the reconstruction and the condition of the limb.

blocks.heading: We start with identifying the problem, not with surgery

body.text: After a complex injury, several causes of impaired function can exist at the same time. It's important to determine which ones need correction, and in what order.
Reconstructing one segment can affect axis, length, gait, and the function of neighboring joints. So planning should not be limited to the area of the old fracture alone.
In multi-stage treatment, every operation should be part of the overall reconstructive plan, not a stand-alone decision.
Complex post-traumatic cases don't always fit a standard scheme. The approach is defined according to the patient's specific anatomy, defect, and functional needs.

blocks.heading: Clinical case: reconstruction of a large post-traumatic tibial defect

body.text: A patient with a severe injury to the right lower leg and a significant bone and soft-tissue defect. After the initial surgical treatment, a large segmental tibial defect had formed.

In a situation like this, the task is no longer simply stabilizing the fracture. It's necessary to restore the missing bone segment, preserve limb length and axis, and create the conditions for restoring the limb's weight-bearing function.
X-ray — initial condition / large tibial defect
Distraction osteogenesis and bone transport based on Ilizarov principles were chosen to restore the defect.
The method works by gradually moving a viable segment of the patient's own bone toward the defect. At the same time, new bone tissue — the regenerate — forms in the distraction zone.
In this way, the patient's own body is effectively used to gradually restore the missing segment with the patient's own bone tissue.
X-ray — bone transport stage in an external fixation frame

blocks.heading: Why this is a lengthy treatment

body.text: Reconstructing large defects with distraction osteogenesis is not a single operation but a lengthy, staged process.

The bone segment must be moved gradually, with ongoing monitoring of regenerate formation, segment position, and limb axis, and after transport is complete, sufficient remodeling and consolidation of the newly formed bone must be awaited.
This is why treating large post-traumatic defects requires not just a correctly performed operation, but a consistent reconstructive strategy and long-term follow-up.
After completing reconstructive treatment and removing the frame, continuity of the tibia was restored and the limb was preserved.

The final X-rays show pronounced post-traumatic bone remodeling in the reconstruction zone. In such complex cases, the goal of treatment is not to create a "perfect" radiographic picture, but to restore a weight-bearing segment and the greatest possible function of the limb.
Final X-ray after frame removal
Large post-traumatic bone defects have no single universal treatment method.

In some situations the optimal solution may be distraction osteogenesis and bone transport; in others, bone grafting, internal fixation, individualized 3D implants, or a combination of several reconstructive methods.
The goal of reconstruction is not simply to close the defect on an X-ray, but to restore a weight-bearing, functional limb.

blocks.heading: If a fracture has already healed incorrectly, can anything be fixed?

body.text: In many cases — yes.
The possibility of correction depends on the nature and location of the deformity, the condition of the bone tissue, joints, and soft tissues, and the overall function of the limb.
To do this, the parameters of the deformity first need to be accurately determined and the correction planned.

blocks.heading: How long should I wait if a fracture isn't healing?

body.text: There is no universal time frame for all fractures. Healing speed depends on the location, the nature of the injury, tissue condition, the method of fixation, and many other factors.
If follow-up examinations don't show the expected progress, or if pain and instability persist, the situation should be reassessed.

blocks.heading: Does old hardware always need to be removed?

body.text: No.

The decision depends on its position, stability, the type of planned reconstruction, and other factors. In some situations the hardware needs to be replaced or removed; in others it can remain part of the treatment.

blocks.heading: Can leg shortening after a fracture be corrected?

body.text: In certain clinical situations — yes.
The method depends on the degree of shortening, the presence of an accompanying deformity, the condition of the bone, and the patient's functional needs.

blocks.heading: Can a deformity be corrected and the limb lengthened at the same time?

body.text: In some cases this is possible.
But whether single-stage or staged correction is appropriate is decided individually, after assessing the anatomy and the complexity of the reconstruction.

blocks.heading: I've already had several operations — is it worth coming in again?

body.text: The number of previous operations alone does not determine whether further treatment is possible.
What matters more is the current condition of the bone, soft tissues, and joints, the presence of infection, the nature of the deformity, and the functional potential of the limb.

blocks.heading: Can full functional recovery be guaranteed?

body.text: No. With complex post-traumatic conditions, the outcome depends on the severity of the original injury, the condition of the tissues, joints, nerves, and vessels, the number of previous operations, and other factors.
The goal of a consultation is to determine a realistic outcome to aim for in a specific situation.

blocks.heading: Is reconstruction always done in a single operation?

body.text: No.
Some deformities can be corrected in a single stage. Complex defects, infectious complications, and combined problems may require several sequential stages.

blocks.heading: What examinations should I bring to the consultation?

body.text: It's best to bring previous X-rays, CT scans or other imaging, discharge summaries from operations, and information about any hardware that was placed.
This helps reconstruct the treatment history and better understand the current problem.
If some documents are missing, the necessary scope of additional examinations can be determined after an in-person assessment.

blocks.heading: The injury is behind you, but the problem remains?

body.text: If pain, deformity, shortening, limping, or restricted function persist after a fracture or previous operations, this doesn't always mean that treatment options have run out.
During the consultation, we'll review your previous treatment, assess the current condition of the limb, and identify possible reconstruction options.
With complex post-traumatic conditions, the first task is to understand what can realistically be restored and how to achieve it.

bone-defects.title: Reconstruction of Critical Bone Defects
bone-defects.lead: Complex reconstructive surgery for significant bone loss following injuries, infections, and previous surgical interventions — with individualized planning and staged limb reconstruction.
bone-defects.intro: Loss of a substantial segment of bone is one of the most challenging problems in reconstructive orthopedics. But even a large bone defect doesn't always mean the possibility of restoring the limb has run out.

blocks.heading: What a critical bone defect is

body.text: After a high-energy injury, an open fracture, an infection, or repeated operations, a situation can arise where part of the bone is effectively lost.

Bone tissue can heal small defects on its own under the right conditions. With significant bone loss, however, the natural healing potential may not be enough, and a dedicated reconstructive strategy is needed to restore bone continuity.

The problem often isn't limited to the size of the defect alone. At the same time, it's necessary to assess limb stability, the condition of the soft tissues, blood supply, the presence of infection, previous operations, and the function of neighboring joints.
That's why treating these patients requires not a single operation, but a plan for reconstructing the limb as a whole.

items: a significant segment of bone was lost after an injury
a bone defect remained after an open or comminuted fracture
part of a bone had to be removed because of infection
a fracture has not healed for a long time due to a defect
several operations have already been performed, but bone continuity has not been restored
a cement spacer or other temporary construct has been placed
there is significant limb shortening after bone tissue loss
complex multi-stage treatment has been proposed and you need an assessment of possible reconstruction options

blocks.heading: Can a large bone defect be restored?

body.text: In many cases, reconstruction is possible even with significant bone tissue loss.
But there is no single method that suits every defect.
The approach depends on:

items: the location and size of the defect
its underlying cause
the condition of the remaining bone
the condition of the soft tissues
the presence or absence of infection
limb length and axis
the condition of the joints
previous operations
the overall functional potential of the limb

body.text: So the key question isn't only "how many centimeters of bone are missing?" but whether the conditions for a stable, functional limb reconstruction can be created.
Depending on the initial situation, treatment may be aimed at:

items: restoring bone continuity
replacing a significant bone defect
creating stable support
restoring limb length and axis
achieving union
controlling an infectious process
improving the limb's ability to bear weight
preserving the limb and restoring its function as fully as possible

body.text: With complex defects, it isn't always possible to fully restore the anatomy that existed before the injury. That's why it's important, even at the planning stage, to define a realistic functional goal for treatment.

blocks.heading: Why treatment often happens in several stages

body.text: With critical defects, trying to solve every problem in a single operation isn't always the best approach.
If there is infection, nonviable tissue, instability, or a significant defect, it may first be necessary to create safe conditions for further reconstruction.
Treatment may include:
infection control and removal of nonviable tissue ↓ temporary stabilization and/or defect replacement ↓ preparation of the bone and soft tissues ↓ definitive reconstruction ↓ functional recovery
The number and sequence of stages are determined individually.
A temporary construct in this situation is not the final result — it's part of the overall treatment plan.
Various reconstructive techniques exist for replacing large bone defects.
Depending on the clinical situation, the following may be considered:

items: bone grafting
